tokyo_restaurant_azuma_ginza.vegan_detail: Not vegan. Pork, beef and egg dishes throughout: jūjū-yaki, hamburg, omurice, pork cutlet; the soup is a beef bouillon.
tokyo_restaurant_azuma_ginza.hours_raw: Daily 11:20–21:00 (L.O. 20:30, Sundays and holidays 20:10); 30 December and 3 January to 16:00; closed 31 December–2 January (Tabelog). Seat reservations carry a ¥350 charge and a two-hour limit (shop site). Cards, IC and QR accepted.
tokyo_restaurant_azuma_ginza.notes: [Yōshoku · since 1946] A town Western-food restaurant founded in 1946, with seating down into the basement. The dish that has been on the menu since the start is jūjū-yaki, sizzling and served in a house-made sauce; one 2026 diner's speciality order was grilled mochi-buta pork. Also on the menu are runny omurice, hamburg, Neapolitan, tonkatsu, a pork 'jambalaya' of ketchup rice with a cutlet (¥1,650 in 2026), fried rice, and an 'adult's kids' lunch' of hamburg and Neapolitan under a flag. Lunch with rice and soup from ¥1,400 (shop site). Drinking-party courses too. A regular notes the Shinjuku branch has closed, leaving this one.

chef_bio.origin: Opened 1 April 1946 (Tabelog); a Shinjuku branch has since closed (2026 review)
chef_bio.background: The shop site calls it a yōshoku restaurant founded in 1946 serving the jūjū-yaki it has served since opening. No source names the owner.
chef_bio.specialty: Jūjū-yaki with house sauce; omurice; Azuma spaghetti.

A diner back after about 25 years ordered the famous jūjū-yaki again.
"With the Shinjuku branch now closed, this Ginza location is truly a gem" — and staff still set dishes down "quite intense and thrilling".

tokyo_cafe_de_lambre_ginza.gf_detail: The shop serves only coffee — staff ask "We only serve coffee, is that alright?" — so there is no food to worry about. Plain black coffee contains no gluten. The Blanc et Noir adds sugar, a little caramel and evaporated milk; ask about any flavoured drink.
tokyo_cafe_de_lambre_ginza.vegan_detail: Coffee only. Black coffee (e.g. Café Noir) is plant-only; the signature Blanc et Noir is topped with evaporated milk, and milk is offered with other drinks.
tokyo_cafe_de_lambre_ginza.hours_raw: Tue–Sat 11:00–20:00; Sun 11:00–18:00; closed Mondays (Tabelog). No cards; iD and PayPay accepted. Coffee only; non-smoking.
tokyo_cafe_de_lambre_ginza.notes: [Mom & Pop · coffee only since 1948] A coffee-only shop that opened in Ginza in 1948, three years after the war, and for coffee people a place of pilgrimage. Founder Sekiguchi Ichirō, who pioneered 'old coffee' (green beans aged ten years or more before roasting), died in 2018 at 103. His nephew Hayashi Fujihiko, who was in and out of the shop as a child and working there before twenty, now runs it. The ice-box fridge and the balance scale with brass weights date from opening day and are still used to weigh every order. Hayashi pours from an enamel pot while moving the flannel dripper, into a small hammered-copper pan made by a regular. The signature is No. 7, Blanc et Noir, 'Queen of Amber': sweetened coffee chilled in a shaker, poured into a champagne glass and floated with evaporated milk (¥850 single in 2021); Café Noir blend ¥750. A cowbell rings as the door opens; in 2026 the small room fills with overseas visitors.

chef_bio.chef_name: 林不二彦 (Hayashi Fujihiko, owner) — founder 関口一郎 (Sekiguchi Ichirō, died 2018 aged 103)
chef_bio.origin: Opened 1948 in Ginza; founder died 2018 aged 103
chef_bio.background: Hayashi is the nephew of founder Sekiguchi Ichirō, about fifty years his junior. He spent childhood summers at the shop, began working there before twenty, and took it over "a long time ago" as a natural course rather than out of passion.
chef_bio.philosophy: 「モタモタやっていたらおいしいものもおいしくないでしょう？ 同じ味でも手際良く出した方が、ね」 — be quick; slow service spoils good coffee.
chef_bio.specialty: Aged old coffee; Blanc et Noir (Queen of Amber); flannel-drip blends.

anecdotes.text: Asked why they still use the ice-box fridge and weight scale from 1948: 「壊れないから」 — "because they don't break."
The copper pan that catches the coffee was designed by a pot-maker who used to come in as a customer.
"Upon entering, the staff asked, 'We only serve coffee, is that alright?'" — October 2026.

tokyo_kissa_kinohana_ginza.gf_detail: Ask. The lunch curries come with naan or rice: choose rice, but the curry ingredients are not published. Cakes such as the cheesecake and lemon meringue tart normally contain wheat. Coffee is brewed fresh by hand.
tokyo_kissa_kinohana_ginza.vegan_detail: Ask. The bean and vegetable curry (yellow split peas) and the eggplant keema are spiced curries from a recipe left by a young Indian cook, but no source says whether they use ghee, dairy or meat stock; "keema" is usually minced meat. Black coffee is plant-only.
tokyo_kissa_kinohana_ginza.hours_raw: Mon, Tue, Wed, Fri, Sat 11:30–18:30 (L.O. 18:00); holidays 12:00–17:30; closed Thursdays and Sundays (Tabelog). No cards; e-money and QR accepted.
tokyo_kissa_kinohana_ginza.notes: [Mom & Pop · the John & Yoko kissaten] Up a narrow, steep stair at the corner behind the Kabuki-za, Narusawa Hiroko opened Kinohana in 1979. She had always wanted work of her own, helped at a friend's restaurant once her children were older, and then studied coffee and café management. On 4 August 1979, its fourth day, Yoko Ono walked in, then John Lennon. Their handwritten note still hangs on the wall, and Beatles fans visit as a pilgrimage. The name comes from a book on her shelf; she loves mountain walking. Beans are delivered from the roaster every other day, ground to order and hand-dripped from a copper kettle (her teacher's habit; this is the third kettle), and she tastes every cup before it goes out. About twenty years in, a young Indian man she met through friends left a curry recipe, and the curries now fill the lunch hour: bean and vegetable curry ¥1,100 and eggplant keema, with salad and coffee for about ¥650 more (2026). Her friend has made the cheesecake since opening. There is also a John Lennon set (¥1,150).

chef_bio.origin: Opened in summer 1979 (4 August was its fourth day); Ginza 4-13-1 2F
chef_bio.background: Long wanted work of her own; after her children grew up she helped at a friend's restaurant, then attended a school for coffee brewing and café management before opening.
chef_bio.philosophy: Fresh beans every other day, ground and hand-dripped to order; she tastes each cup before serving.
chef_bio.specialty: Original blends from a copper kettle; Indian-style curries; cheesecake.

anecdotes.text: 「ドアが開いたから、『いらっしゃいませ』と顔を向けたらオノ・ヨーコさんが最初に入っていらっしゃって、その後にジョン・レノンさん。本当にびっくり」 — 4 August 1979, the fourth day.
Once, exhausted after late-night prep, she jumped on the last train from Higashi-Ginza and found it going the wrong way.
The book designer Kikuchi Nobuyoshi used 『樹の花』 as the title of one of his books.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: さんたつ(2021.6.24): 樹の花、木挽町通りと松屋通りの角のビル2階、店主・成沢弘子さん、1979年開店、4日目の8月4日にジョン・レノンとオノ・ヨーコが来店(直筆の便箋)、店名は山歩きが好きな成沢さんの手元の本から、焙煎所から1日おきに豆、銅製のやかん(3代目)、オリジナルブレンド700円から、なすのキーマカレー&ナンorライス1,200円、インド人青年のレシピのカレー、創業当時から友人の作るチーズケーキ、装丁家菊地信義の著書名。食べログ: 月火水金土11:30〜18:30、祝12:00〜17:30、木日休。2026年の口コミ: 豆と野菜のカレー1,100円(+650円でサラダとコーヒー)、ジョン・レノンセット1,150円、レモンメレンゲタルトのセット1,470円。

tokyo_juichibo_coffee_ginza.gf_detail: Ask. Black coffee, roasted and brewed in house, contains no gluten. The cakes (chocolate cake, chiffon cake with dried fruit and nuts) normally contain wheat, and no ingredients are published.
tokyo_juichibo_coffee_ginza.vegan_detail: Black coffee is plant-only; royal milk tea and the cakes contain dairy or egg as usually made. No vegan item is described.
tokyo_juichibo_coffee_ginza.hours_raw: Daily 11:00–21:30 (Tabelog). Cash only. No groups of four or more; a quiet room.
tokyo_juichibo_coffee_ginza.notes: [Mom & Pop · nel-drip coffee since 1978] A grown-up coffee house near the Yūrakubashi crossing: a long single-plank counter, worn leather chairs, jazz, and no groups of four or more. It opened in 1978 in a basement on Yanagi-dōri and moved here about thirty years ago. Owner Hasegawa Yoshikazu began as a regular, went into coffee work, and took it over because he couldn't bear to see it disappear. He roasts everything on a classic 'buta-gama' roaster in the glass booth by the door, taking specialty beans deeper than most, and every cup is brewed through flannel; staff sew the filters themselves in quiet moments. Blends from ¥920 (2025), plus seasonal single origins, royal milk tea, chocolate cake and fruit-and-nut chiffon.

chef_bio.origin: Founded 1978 (basement on Yanagi-dōri); at the present site about 30 years
chef_bio.background: A former regular who later worked in the coffee trade and took over Jūichibō to keep the old shop alive.
chef_bio.philosophy: 「珈琲店が変わらずにあるって大切ですよね」 — a coffee shop that stays the same matters.
chef_bio.specialty: Deep-roasted specialty and classic blends by nel drip.

tokyo_ginza_mikawaya.gf_detail: Not gluten-free. Classic yōshoku: the house gratin (butter rice under prawn cream sauce), crab cream croquettes, beef stew and hamburg, all normally built on wheat roux, breadcrumbs or demi-glace. No gluten-free option is mentioned.
tokyo_ginza_mikawaya.vegan_detail: Not vegan. Seafood, beef and cream dishes throughout: gratin, crab croquette, tongue and beef stew, live sweet-shrimp tempura.
tokyo_ginza_mikawaya.hours_raw: Daily 11:00–21:00 (L.O. 20:00); closed over New Year (Tabelog). Cards accepted. 10% service charge.
tokyo_ginza_mikawaya.notes: [Yōshoku · Sally Weil's lineage] The shop's own history begins in September 1887, when Hosaka Yoshijirō, a descendant of a Mikawa family that served the Tokugawa, opened the Mikawaya grocery next to today's Wakō, drawn in Hiroshige IV's print of Ginza. His successor Hosaka Kōji led the Ginza street association. After the war the former president Tonaka Toyoichirō took over and reopened it as the French restaurant Mikawaya. He was one of a handful taught directly by Sally Weil, first head chef of Yokohama's Hotel New Grand. Its gratin descends from a dish Weil improvised for an unwell guest, butter rice under prawns in cream sauce, browned with cheese, the dish the rest of Japan came to call doria. The house still uses the opening recipes and serves 'French food eaten with chopsticks': pickles with rice dishes and green tea after the meal. Diners order crab cream croquettes, beef or tongue stew, hamburg, omurice, and courses from about ¥11,000; takeaway and mail order sell the croquettes and tongue stew.

roles: restaurant company (former president 渡仲豊一郎 Tonaka Toyoichirō reopened it post-war)
chef_bio.origin: Grocery founded September 1887; reopened as a French restaurant after the war at the present site (Ginza Mitsukoshi annex)
chef_bio.background: Founder Hosaka Yoshijirō (三河屋食料品店, 1887); successor Hosaka Kōji; post-war, former president Tonaka Toyoichirō, a direct pupil of Sally Weil (Hotel New Grand). Tabelog lists a corporate invoice number (T8010001058013).
chef_bio.philosophy: 〝お箸で食べるフランス料理を〟 — French cooking eaten with chopsticks, with pickles and green tea.
chef_bio.specialty: Original gratin; crab cream croquette; tongue stew.

anecdotes.text: 「体調が良くないので、何かのど越しの良いものを」 — the request that, the shop says, led Weil to improvise butter rice with prawn cream sauce under cheese, the origin of its gratin.
創業時の姿は浮世絵師：四代広重の「銀座繁昌之図」の中にも描かれています.
A September 2026 diner returned after four years for the white sauce, "exceptional", on the ¥11,000 course.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: 公式(ginza-mikawaya.com 歴史): 明治20年(1887)9月、保坂芳次郎が和光の隣に「三河屋食料品店」を開業(四代広重「銀座繁昌之図」)、後継者・保坂幸治は銀座通連合会会長、終戦後に元社長・渡仲豊一郎が受け継ぎ現在地に「フランス料理 みかわや」として再興、ホテルニューグランド初代料理長S.ワイルの直伝、グラタン(ドリアの原型)、創業当時のレシピ、お箸で食べるフランス料理、漬物と緑茶。食べログ: 銀座4-7-12 銀座三越新館1階、42席、毎日11:00〜21:00、サービス料10%。2026年の口コミ: 11,000円のコース、かにクリームコロッケ、ビーフシチュー、ハンバーグ、オムライス、活き甘海老の天ぷら。

cultural_comfort.note: A classic, quiet dining room on the Mitsukoshi annex ground floor; chopsticks offered. Cards; 10% service charge; terrace seats allow pets.

tokyo_kissa_american_ginza.gf_detail: Not gluten-free. The whole menu is sandwiches on soft white bread baked that day, egg, potato and others, in loaf-sized portions. No gluten-free option is mentioned.
tokyo_kissa_american_ginza.vegan_detail: Not vegan. The signature egg sandwich is filled with boiled-egg filling (the special uses about eight eggs); the potato sandwich and set soup are not described as egg- or dairy-free.
tokyo_kissa_american_ginza.hours_raw: Mon–Fri 08:30–14:30 (L.O. 14:00); closed Saturdays, Sundays and holidays; closes when the bread runs out (Tabelog). Cash only. Takeaway available.
tokyo_kissa_american_ginza.notes: [Mom & Pop · loaf-sized sandwiches] A New York-deli-looking kissaten in the alley beside the Kabuki-za, opened in 1983. When the theatre was rebuilt, the owner, Haraguchi Makoto, decided the shop needed a signature and made the sandwiches absurdly big: "one serving is a whole loaf." The bread is baked that day and very soft; the boiled-egg filling is fist-sized, and the 'special egg sandwich' uses about eight eggs. Nobody finishes, so wrapping the rest to take home is normal. In 2019 a sandwich set came with a heap of salad, soup and a drink (¥1,200). In 2026 a special egg sandwich with iced coffee was about ¥2,000, and an egg-and-potato takeaway set ¥1,000. The walls are covered in Saga Prefecture posters and signatures. Busy, shared tables, cash only, weekdays only, and it shuts when the bread runs out.

chef_bio.background: The owner made the sandwiches jumbo-sized as a signature at the time of the Kabuki-za rebuilding (san-tatsu, 2019).
chef_bio.philosophy: 「1人前はパン1斤だね」 — one serving is a whole loaf.
chef_bio.specialty: Egg sandwich; special egg sandwich (about eight eggs); potato sandwich.

anecdotes.text: 1983年に創業したこちらは、歌舞伎座の改装を機に名物を作ろうと一大決心。そこで笑っちゃうほどジャンボなサイズにしたという。「1人前はパン1斤だね」。わっはっはと名物店主の原口誠さんは豪快に笑う.
An October 2026 diner, after a night shift, was steered by staff from the regular egg sandwich to the special, "an astonishing volume of 8 eggs".
A second-time diner took a quarter of the special home; at busy times you share a table.

tokyo_cafe_de_ruton_ginza.gf_detail: Ask. Black coffee (aged beans) contains no gluten, but the food is waffles and crêpes, which are wheat-based as usually made. No ingredients are published.
tokyo_cafe_de_ruton_ginza.vegan_detail: Black coffee is plant-only. The waffles and crêpes normally contain egg, milk or butter and are served with fruit and cream; nothing is described as vegan.
tokyo_cafe_de_ruton_ginza.hours_raw: Mon–Fri 11:00–17:00; Sat & Sun 11:00–18:00 (Tabelog, 2026; a 2019 guide listed longer hours). Cash only. Two-hour limit at busy times.
tokyo_cafe_de_ruton_ginza.notes: [Mom & Pop · Art Nouveau basement] Down an unpromising staircase, or a lift, in a plain building a minute from Ginza Station is a surprisingly large, high-ceilinged, hushed room. It is filled with the Art Nouveau furniture, ceramics, antique clocks and stained glass collected by owner Ida Toshimitsu. "Customers change, but the shop doesn't," he told san-tatsu in 2019, when it had been open thirty-eight years. The coffee is mellow, made with aged beans; the Meissen Blend, Brazil-based, was ¥900 in 2019, poured into period cups, and the waffles cost ¥600. In 2026 diners came for banana crêpes topped with peaches and berries (about ¥800) and chocolate waffles, and likened the room to a Studio Ghibli set.

chef_bio.origin: About 38 years at this site as of 2019
chef_bio.background: The owner collected the Art Nouveau furnishings and porcelain that fill the room (san-tatsu, 2019).
chef_bio.philosophy: 「お客さんは変わるけれど、店は変わらない」

tokyo_kissa_fuji_marunouchi.gf_detail: Not gluten-free in practice. The menu is kissaten yōshoku: nine spaghetti dishes, baked curry, omelette curry, hamburg, ginger pork, pilaf and sandwiches, none described as gluten-free. Coffee itself contains no gluten.

tokyo_kissa_fuji_marunouchi.notes: [Mom & Pop · a family kissaten under the viaducts] The ground floor of a free-standing house (a mahjong parlour is upstairs) in the lane between the JR tracks and the Shinkansen viaduct, signposted 'Coffee & Lunch FUJI' with a blue Key Coffee sign. It was founded about 66 years before 2024, just nearby, by the father of the owner's husband, as a drinks-only café, and moved here in 1986. When her husband died, Fujita Keiko, then 45 and a full-time housewife, suddenly became the owner. She has run it for about forty years since, slowly building up the food. When the Tokyo Metropolitan Government was still in Marunouchi, bidders for city contracts used it as their office, and it had a row of public phones. The sasanqua outside was transplanted from the old city-hall streets. Plates are generous: pork sauté of about 250 g of loin with soup and rice (¥1,180), nine spaghetti dishes led by carbonara (¥1,250 with salad, soup and coffee), omelette curry, baked curry, chocolate parfait (¥950), coffee ¥500 (2024 prices). In 2026 two staff handle the lunch rush. Smoking is allowed.

tokyo_kissa_royal_yurakucho.notes: [Kissaten · since 1965] A glittering jun-kissa that opened with the Tokyo Kōtsū Kaikan in 1965, at the foot of the spiral stair to the basement. Its first manager, a businessman who loved luxury, gave it bright red sofas, stained glass and artworks, such as a peacock made only of hearts, and most of that décor survives. The lamps on the dividing poles were once its only light; the room was brightened when older regulars said they couldn't read their newspapers. The floor is run by men in white shirts and ties, aged about fifty to seventy, under the friendly third-generation manager Noyama, and some waiters of twenty years know regulars' names, orders and seats. The seasonal fruit parfait (strawberries, cream and ice cream; melon ¥1,200 in 2026) has been on the menu since opening, alongside a firm kissaten custard pudding with sticky caramel. Blend coffee ¥800. Around 95–120 seats, quick turnover.

tokyo_izakaya_tontonton_yurakucho.notes: [Izakaya · under the tracks since 1953] A red-lantern offal-yakitori bar inside the arched tunnel that runs under the tracks from the Hibiya side to the Ginza side, in the same spot since 1953; trains rumble overhead and the ceiling slopes like an attic. Skewers are threaded from 7:30 each morning for that day and grilled raw over charcoal at the street-side grill: kashira (here skirt, not temple), pork belly with salt, pepper and garlic miso, and tsukune in a tare topped up since opening. Order at least two of each. The beef-offal stew in a house miso (¥630 in 2024) and a Hoisu sour (¥500), the Shōwa-30s shōchū mixer, complete it. Manager Iwamoto Yūji, who has worked in izakaya since fifteen, took over during the tail of COVID. Overseas visitors photograph the place inside and out, and strangers end up talking.

tokyo_chugoku_ryori_horyu_yurakucho.notes: [Mom & Pop · machi-chūka under the tracks] A neighbourhood Chinese restaurant under the JR viaduct by Yūrakuchō's Kyōbashi exit, ten seconds from the station. It opened here in 1967; before that it was a food stall in the 'sushiya yokochō' that stood where the Tokyo Kōtsū Kaikan is now. Owner Uei Keiichi says there's no single best-seller, because regulars all have their own orders, but jokes the free house chilli oil (garlic and chilli, also sold in jars) might be it. Cooks of twenty years and more use different noodles for shōyu, miso and tsukemen, and there are monthly specials. Prices are station-cheap: shōyu ramen ¥650, or ¥750 with half fried rice; noodles ¥650–900, a dozen set meals ¥850–950 with rice, soup, pickles and seasoned nori; gyoza ¥550 with a Sichuan-pepper salt (2025). Open all day without a break.

Orders run from crisp butter toast and a banana milk float with vanilla soft-serve to omu-hayashi and a 'surprising omurice' with a shrimp-and-mushroom risotto inside (¥1,100, 2026). A good escape when the basement queues are long.

tokyo_utaeru_izakaya_honjitsu_kaiten.notes: [Mom & Pop · the sing-along izakaya] At the very back of the Kōtsū Kaikan basement, a neon sign and a noren mark a family izakaya where everyone sings. It began about sixty years before 2024, when the current master's father, a sandwich-board man, opened a snack-bar-cum-pub in the 'sushiya yokochō' that once stood here, hence the karaoke. It moved into the Kōtsū Kaikan around 1967 and kept the name 'Honjitsu Kaiten', 'opening today', the line those sandwich boards always carried: "so as not to forget where we started," master Abe Hisao suspects. He runs it with the mama. Regulars, mostly forty to sixty, sing Ōe Senri, YMO and Godiego and drift between tables. Most of them met here. The master, once a vocalist, will duet with you. The food is home-cooked: vegetable-heavy sauce yakisoba (¥780), black mapo tofu (¥620, or a bowl for ¥130 more), keema curry with chickpeas (¥750), karaage, curry croquettes, grilled stingray fin and oden (2024–2026). Songs cost ¥200 each. First-timers and solo drinkers are welcomed in.

tokyo_cafe_terrace_pont_neuf_shimbashi.notes: [Yōshoku · Napolitan since the Shōwa boom] 'Pont Neuf', French for 'new bridge', so 'Shin-bashi'. It opened in 1967, a year after the Shimbashi Ekimae Building was finished, as an ordinary jun-kissa of coffee, pudding and sandwiches. Under the second manager, in Japan's boom years, it turned to hearty food for Shimbashi's salarymen: Napolitan first, then hamburg spaghetti, the 'Pont Neuf burg' and hamburg sandwiches. The third manager, Uekusa, began in 2007 helping the long-serving ladies wash dishes, and took over in 2018. He thickened the boiled-ahead spaghetti from 2.0 mm to 2.2 mm. The Napolitan is mellow rather than sharp and uses ham, not bacon. The hamburg, beef-and-pork with pepper and garlic, is finished in the oven. Both share an original sauce of minced meat and seasonings. A food critic's praise made the Napolitan famous. In 2026: Napolitan ¥1,100, hamburg spaghetti ¥1,400, and on Friday nights a bacon-and-cheese Napolitan for ¥2,000. Diners call it a 2026 Tabelog top-100 yōshoku shop.

tokyo_taishu_kappo_sanshuya_ginza.notes: [Mom & Pop · the fish diner that never closes for a break] A popular fish house that Okada Masayuki, born 1935, opened in 1968 after training at Kanda Sanshūya. In 2020, past eighty, he was still going to the fish market every morning, Tsukiji and then Toyosu: "there's nowhere else, so what can you do." It long stood in an alley that shielded salarymen who didn't want to be seen drinking at lunchtime. When the old building came down, the shop reopened at Ginza 2-3-4, and it now stands in full view. It runs without a break from morning to night. City-hall staff came at five, newspaper reporters at odd hours. Sit at shared six-seat white-wood tables, the counter or the tatami upstairs, and order from the wall and the whiteboard: thick-cut sashimi sets (¥1,100 in 2020), a seafood bowl on warm rice, oyster-fry sets (¥1,350), and the regulars' favourite chicken-tofu pot with ponzu (¥480). Staff of twenty years and more keep it brisk rather than chatty. A 2021 Tabelog set-meal top-100 pick.

tokyo_bar_lupin_ginza.notes: [Mom & Pop · the literary bar since 1928] A basement bar opened in 1928 by Takasaki Yukiko, a popular hostess at Café Tiger who struck out on her own with the backing of writers Kikuchi Kan, Satomi Ton, Izumi Kyōka and Kume Masao. It became a counter bar in 1935, and the slab of yachidamo ash on the counter has been in use ever since. Hayashi Tadahiko's photographs of Dazai Osamu, Sakaguchi Ango and Oda Sakunosuke sitting cross-legged here hang on the wall. It was bombed in January 1945, renamed 麺包亭 to avoid an 'enemy' word, closed, and reopened after the war as a café pouring black-market drink. When the building was rebuilt in 1972, every fixture was stored and the room rebuilt to the same layout. Yukiko worked the bar until about 1981. Her grandson Takasaki Naohiko now manages it, and bartender Hiraki Ikuo shakes Ango's Golden Fizz (egg yolk, lemon) and pours from shot glasses dating to 1928. In 2026 the room fills with fans of the anime Bungō Stray Dogs alongside old regulars. Try the Thunderclap: brandy, whisky and gin.

tokyo_tonkatsu_akebono_yurakucho.notes: [Mom & Pop · katsudon from the すしや横丁] Nakamura Bunzō's father opened a canteen in 1962 in the 'sushiya yokochō', the shanty strip of sushi bars, drinking dens and offal stalls facing Yūrakuchō Station's tracks. When the Kōtsū Kaikan replaced it, the shop came underground. In the city-hall days lunch was mobbed with civil servants and there was no day off. When the government moved out, the area's restaurants thinned and times were hard. "Customers kept coming to see my cheerful father and mother — I'm only copying them," Nakamura says. Domestic pork from his father's suppliers is trimmed, coated in coarse fresh crumbs and fried in hot lard, then simmered with tare and egg over pot-cooked domestic rice. The katsudon comes with niboshi miso soup and house pickles for ¥1,000 (2025; ¥1,100 in an October 2026 review), a remarkable price facing the station. There is also a mixed fry set of fillet cutlet, fried shrimp and fried horse mackerel. In October 2026 a dozen people were queuing before the 11:00 opening. Write your order on the mini whiteboard at the door. There are eleven counter seats. A small onigiri comes while you wait, and Nakamura serves bigger portions than his father did: 'I'm short-sighted,' he jokes.

tokyo_yukun_sakagura_shimbashi.gf_detail: Not gluten-free in practice. Kyūshū dishes such as sashimi with sweet Kyūshū soy sauce and black-pork skewers glazed in a sweet soy tare; courses mix many dishes. No gluten-free option is mentioned.
tokyo_yukun_sakagura_shimbashi.vegan_detail: Not vegan as a restaurant: horse sashimi, kibinago and other fish, gameni with chicken, black-pork skewers. Grilled eggplant is one of the few plant dishes mentioned, and its seasoning is not described.
tokyo_yukun_sakagura_shimbashi.hours_raw: Tue–Fri 17:00–23:00 (L.O. 22:00); Sat 16:30–23:00 (L.O. 22:00); closed Sundays, Mondays (open in December), holidays, Obon and New Year (Tabelog). Booking strongly advised; the phone line is closed, so book online. Visa and Mastercard accepted.
tokyo_yukun_sakagura_shimbashi.notes: [Mom & Pop · the high-school reunion izakaya] A basement izakaya on Sotobori-dōri opened in 1978 by Fukuoka-born owner Matsunaga Tomokazu and run with his wife, okami Matsunaga Yōko. Ingredients are flown in from Kyūshū daily, but since the Isahaya Bay sea-gates cut off its Ariake Sea supply it no longer insists on Kyūshū alone and buys fresh fish from Kantō and Tōhoku too. The menu still leans Kyūshū: Kumamoto horse sashimi that has never been frozen, kibinago sashimi, gameni (chikuzen-ni, chicken and vegetables simmered in dashi, ¥1,050 in 2024) and black-pork belly skewers in a sweet soy tare (¥800), with sweet Kyūshū soy sauce and Fukuoka's 'Yūkun' daiginjō from Takahashi Shuzō. It is famous for something else, though: since opening, guests have filled 'high-school message notebooks', one per school, now more than 3,400 of Japan's 4,874 high schools (MEXT, 2020). The first, in 1987, was for Kurume University Fuzoku High School, started for a regular who came 300 days a year. Write your school on the memo the staff bring and they will fetch its notebook from the index. Alumni book it out nightly; courses such as the 'High School Freshman' (¥3,800 in 2026) keep a reunion simple.

tokyo_tachinomi_kuri_shimbashi.gf_detail: A standing sake bar. Sake itself is brewed from rice and contains no wheat, but beer and Hoppy are barley-based, and the snacks (pickles, dressed dishes, inari, potato salad) are not described ingredient by ingredient. Ask.
tokyo_tachinomi_kuri_shimbashi.vegan_detail: Ask. The okami's potato salad contains boiled egg. The inari (sushi rice with red pickled ginger in sweet-savoury simmered fried tofu) may suit, but how the tofu is simmered is not described, so ask about dashi.

tokyo_tachinomi_kuri_shimbashi.notes: [Standing sake bar · the Kurihara family's sake shop] A standing sake bar on the ground floor of the Shimbashi Ekimae Building, opened on 22 May 2012, the same day as Tokyo Skytree, by さかや栗原, a family sake shop based in Minami-Naruse, Machida. The eldest son now runs the shop, and the second son runs the sister 和酒Pub 庫裏 in the basement of the same building. The walls are lined with framed sake labels from all 47 prefectures, collected by okami Kurihara Itsuko since 1983, when she married into the shop, and sent unglued and unused by the breweries; some breweries and brands no longer exist. About 30 seasonal and 10 aged sakes are poured 80 ml at a time for ¥300–1,000, and the okami will pick one to suit a beginner. The three-glass omakase set is ¥1,000 (2024 and 2026). Snacks are mostly pickles and dressed dishes at ¥100–350. Those marked '伊', for Itsuko, are made by the okami every day: inari tinted pink with chopped red ginger (¥200), a potato salad with boiled egg whose dressing changes for the regulars (¥100), and seasoned eggs. Pay as you go: one 2024 evening came to exactly ¥1,000. In October 2026 diners praised the range for the price, including Ishikawa's Fukumasamune and Miyagi's Suminoe. It is one of a small group of 庫裏 sake bars in Shimbashi and Ginza: a 2012 reviewer called it the group's third shop, and Retty also lists a 和酒BAR 庫裏 in Ginza.

tokyo_ginza_torishige.gf_detail: Ask. Charcoal-grilled chicken comes both salt-grilled (shio) and with the house tare, and the meal ends with the signature dry curry. No source gives the ingredients of the tare or the dry curry. The shop asks guests to mention allergies when booking.
tokyo_ginza_torishige.vegan_detail: Ask. A chicken yakitori shop, and the courses are built around chicken and duck, but the à la carte list has charcoal-grilled vegetables (leek, shishitō, okra, ginkgo, shiitake, tomato, manganji pepper). Seasoning and shared grills are not described.
tokyo_ginza_torishige.hours_raw: Mon–Fri 17:00–22:00; Sat 16:00–21:00; closed Sundays, holidays, fifth Saturdays, Golden Week, and summer and winter breaks (official site). Food L.O. around 20:00. Reservations are for courses only and online only; the phone line is closed. Cards, e-money and d Barai accepted (Tabelog).
tokyo_ginza_torishige.notes: [Mom & Pop · the 1931 yakitori stall] In 1931 the founder 保立繁之助, a trained kappō cook, and his wife なか pulled a yakitori stall out from behind the Kabukiza every night and set it up in the Kōjunsha's fuel yard, where kabuki actors and Ginza's cultural crowd ate. The stall became a shop in 1939, passed to the second generation, and moved to its present site in 1958. It is now in the third generation; the Tabelog shop page describes three generations 'showcasing the strong family bonds'. The skewers are large and grilled over charcoal: duck, chicken wings, tsukune both in tare and with salt, liver, skin (¥600–850 each), and from 15 November to 15 February wild duck, teal and moorhen. The famous finish is the dry curry. The founder first made it as a staff meal, with curry powder a customer brought as a gift, before curry rice was common. Staff ask about it with your first order so they know how much rice to cook. Sake is warmed in a pure-silver kettle and poured from a height. Courses are ¥8,600 (90th-anniversary) and ¥9,500 (duck loin) from January 2025. Dry curry with chicken soup is ¥1,000 and can be taken home.
